item.description:

item.title: The Lifespan and the Dragon Girl: The One Vehicle and the Open Sky, Part Five
item.description:
The Lotus Sutra breaks its own clock, twice. An eight-year-old naga's daughter attains Buddhahood in a single moment while the old order watches in silence, and the Buddha reveals a lifespan that outlasts the math of dust atoms: his awakening was countless eons ago, and his death itself is skillful means. The part ends where the sutra says the triple world is not born and does not die, the Great Perfection's ground in the Lotus's own words. item.title: The Man Who Wanted Never to Come Down: Ram Dass, Neem Karoli Baba, and the Work of Coming Back
item.description:
Richard Alpert had everything the American dream could measure, and it was not enough. Twenty chapters follow him through Harvard and psychedelics to a blanket-wrapped teacher in the Indian hills, and through the fifty years after: devotion, service, error, stroke, and the work of coming back. Hanuman, bhakti, Maharajji's remembered teachings on Christ, Siddhi Ma and the labor of community keep the Indian devotional world visible beyond its American narrator. Miracle accounts are identified as testimony, not scientific or medical proof. No drug-use advice, no claims of cure. The closing reflection is original commentary, not a transmitted practice.

item.description:

A sentence that reaches us opens a study of translation as shared responsibility. Vairotsana's remembered life leads through collaborative translation, vocabulary, canonical credit, revision, journey and exile, a female teacher, nonduality and ethics, a royal funeral contest, cultural brokerage and the courage to let another person correct us. The translator is distinguished from the Buddha Vairocana. The funeral contest is not the Samye debate.

item.title: Kant: The Law Within
item.description:
An eight-chapter guided course on Immanuel Kant: the clock of Königsberg and the young Kant of Swedenborg and Rousseau, the Copernican turn (synthetic a priori, space and time, appearances and things in themselves), the machinery of the categories and the walls of reason (causality, the antinomies, the God proofs, the three questions), the Groundwork's good will and categorical imperative, the fact of reason and the starry heavens, the third Critique on beauty and the sublime, the crooked timber of the political essays, and Kant's inheritance, with one explicitly labeled Buddhist comparison as a reading lantern. Narrated by Tara, an AI voice, with a special appearance by guest narrator Muse in five sections, volume matched. All primary works read from public-domain translations: the Groundwork and Prolegomena in full; the three Critiques, Religion, Dreams of a Spirit-Seer and the political essays in substantial selections; the Enlightenment essay in German with the course's own renderings, labeled. Anecdotes are labeled: the watch-setting walk and the Emile interruption are posthumous biographical tradition; the Swedenborg ghost stories are Kant's own hearsay report. Quoted material preserves the source translations' exact wording (for example, "requirest submission" in the Critique of Practical Reason passage); the surrounding narration modernizes archaic inflection. item.title: Plato: The Examined Life
item.description:
From Socrates's trial to the invisible ring, the divided soul, the cave and the philosopher-rulers: an introduction to Plato that takes the arguments seriously without excusing their political costs. Includes Diotima's account of love, the Phaedrus on writing, a source-honest translation note, and the myth of Er. History, dramatic presentation, myth and interpretation are kept distinct. Narrated by Tara, an AI voice. Provisional interpretation, not an authoritative translation, lineage transmission or practice authorization.
Full primary works read: the Apology and Crito in Benjamin Jowett's public-domain translation; the Republic, Symposium and Phaedrus appear as selected passages only, and the course says so - no whole-corpus claim. Socrates in the dialogues is a dramatic speaker, not a verbatim recording of the historical man. The oracle, the ring of Gyges, the cave, Diotima's account of Love's parentage, the Egyptian writing story and the myth of Er are attributed to their dramatic contexts, not treated as verified events. Moral and political criticism, present-day illustrations and the closing exercise are the course author's own interpretation and application. No long quotations; every argument is given in the course's own words. Original narration and commentary CC0 1.0 Universal.

Aryadeva, traditionally called Madhyamaka's second founder: the Sri Lankan prince of the biographies, the gift of an eye, the one-eyed verse that challenges three-eyed Shiva, and a debate legend ending in conversion. item.title: Spinoza: God or Nature
item.description:
An own-words introduction to Baruch Spinoza: the excommunicated lens grinder of Amsterdam, the Ethics built like geometry from definitions to blessedness, God or Nature, the mind as the body's idea, the emotions as physics, the Treatise that argues freedom of thought and speech is the foundation of every free state, the long afterlife from herem to Einstein, an honest side-by-side with Buddhist philosophy - where the two genuinely meet and where they do not - and a reading guide to the translations. Narrated by Tara, an AI voice. Provisional interpretation, not an authoritative translation, lineage transmission or practice authorization.
All quotations from Spinoza are read in R. H. M. Elwes's 1883 translation (public domain, Project Gutenberg #3800 and #989) and were verified verbatim against those texts; the Ethics definitions and propositions and the Theological-Political Treatise preface quotes follow Elwes's wording exactly. Biographical claims were checked against the standard public record (the Spinoza House biography and the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy), and the one episode where the record is uncertain - how close Spinoza stood to Jan de Witt - is stated as uncertain in the episode. The chapter on Buddhism is an interpretive comparison, not a claim of historical contact or influence, and its disagreements are stated as disagreements. Original narration and commentary CC0 1.0 Universal.
